query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state, local chemical short-range ordering during high-temperature service promotes the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that disrupt the formation of a uniform, protective oxide layer, leading to reduced corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution state with a uniform initial oxide film upon exposure.
generation.intervention: Perform in situ high-temperature environmental TEM or synchrotron XRD under controlled oxidizing conditions.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant thermal conditions (approximately 500–900°C) in an oxidizing atmosphere with appropriate oxygen partial pressure.
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates arising from local chemical short-range order.
generation.mechanism: At service temperatures, local chemical fluctuations concentrate Mg which nucleates as Mg-rich intermetallic phases. Their growth interrupts the continuity of the passivating oxide layer, compromising its protective function and thereby accelerating oxidation and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial state, the alloy will exhibit dispersed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates accompanied by localized disruptions or discontinuities in the protective oxide scale, leading to measurable increases in oxidation and corrosion rates.
generation.baseline: The initial metastable solid solution state with a uniform, adherent oxide layer that provides effective corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: Observations are expected when the alloy is exposed to temperatures between 500 and 900°C in oxidizing environments typical of high-temperature service conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise nucleation kinetics, the critical volume fraction of intermetallics required to disrupt the oxide layer, and the spatiotemporal evolution of these features remain to be quantitatively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in situ high-temperature environmental TEM (or synchrotron XRD) experiments on the metastable alloy under controlled oxidizing conditions within the 500–900°C range. Monitor the evolution of the microstructure in real time, focusing on the onset and growth of Mg-rich precipitates and any concomitant disruptions in the oxide layer.
measurements: Real-time imaging of microstructural changes to detect nucleation and growth of intermetallic phases.
EDS mapping to confirm local chemical composition variations (Mg enrichment) at the precipitate sites.
Analysis of oxide layer continuity and composition changes over time.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no distinct Mg-rich intermetallic phases are observed to nucleate and grow, or if the protective oxide layer remains continuous and shows no correlation with any intermetallic formation during the entire service-relevant temperature exposure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are among the promising candidates for the design of structural materials in advanced nuclear energy systems. The effects of Cr, V, Ta, and Ti elements and ball milling on the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of model RHEAs were investigated. The results show that W-rich BCC1 and Ta-rich BCC2 solid solution phases were generated after a long milling duration. After high-temperature sintering, the (Cr, Ta)-rich phase associated with the Laves phase was observed in the Cr-containing model RHEAs. In addition, a high level of Ti, Ta, and V contents promoted the in situ formation of oxide particles in the alloys. Complex TiTa2O7 and Ta2VO6 oxide phases were identified by TEM, which suggests a solid-state reaction of Ti-O, Ta-O, and V-O subjected to high-energy ball milling. The oxide particles are uniformly dispersed in the BCC matrix, which can result in dispersion strengthening and the enhancement of mechanical properties.

cited_evidence.text: As observed during the isothermal oxidation process, the outer oxide layers of the FeNiCuAlCo and FeNiCuAlMn HEAs develop wrinkles, while the inner oxide layers bend and may even detach from the substrate (Figure 7b,c), leading to the formation of an irregular oxide layer. In contrast, the oxide film of the FeNiCuAlCr HEA is denser and remains free of cracks. Figure 8 is a schematic of the oxidation mechanism of FeNiCuAlCr alloys in air at 900 °C. In the oxidation process of FeNiCuAlCr high-entropy alloys, Al2O3 initially forms on the surface, where it acts as a passivating layer, preventing further oxygen diffusion and thereby limiting the oxidation of internal elements. Subsequently, chromium oxide and copper oxide layers form. As the oxidation progresses, the Al2O3 and Cr2O3 oxide layers grow thicker and merge, with oxygen gradually migrating inward. Over time, under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the system reaches local equilibrium in oxygen partial pressure, leading to the formation of continuous spinel-type oxides (NiFe2O4) due to reactions between Ni and Fe oxides. These factors contribute to the excellent high-temperature oxidation resistance of FeNiCuAlCr alloys.

decision.trend: Beginning in 2020, studies of lightweight Al-Mg-based complex concentrated alloys revealed the formation of intermetallic phases upon heat treatment, which can compromise mechanical properties and environmental resistance (PMC7579168::webcard). By 2024, researchers showed that high-pressure processing of an Al55Mg35Li5Zn5 alloy could help retain a single-phase solid solution, improving specific strength but leaving the question of how to preserve those advantages under standard service conditions (PMC11330973::webcard). By 2025, attention broadened to nonequilibrium phenomena such as chemical short-range order, offering new insights into how effective resistance to corrosion/oxidation might be lost or maintained during microstructural evolution from a metastable state (PMC12508472::webcard). Despite these advances, the exact transformation pathways and kinetics driving secondary phase formation and its impact on corrosion and oxidation remain inadequately understood in Mg-containing high-entropy alloys.
decision.unsolved: How Mg-rich intermetallics nucleate and grow from a metastable solid solution, and thereby affect protective oxide formation and corrosion behavior, remains unclear. The interplay of nonequilibrium states, potential short-range ordering, and intermetallic nucleation under real operating temperatures and environments has yet to be conclusively demonstrated or falsified.
decision.lever: Perform in situ high-temperature environmental TEM (or synchrotron XRD) on the metastable Mg-containing alloy under service-relevant thermal and corrosive conditions, tracking the onset and progression of any evolving second phases, local chemical variations, and changes in oxide-layer stability compared to the initial solutionized state.
decision.why: Direct, in situ observation of microstructural transformations and real-time measurements of corrosion/oxidation behavior at service temperatures can pinpoint whether metastable decomposition to Mg-rich intermetallic phases leads to breakdown of the protective oxide or passivation layer, explaining potential loss of environmental resistance. If no distinct precipitation or passivation breakdown is observed, the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.
